nameStory: The Florida pompano gets its name from the Spanish word 'pámpana,' meaning vine leaf, referring to its broad, flattened body shape that resembles a large leaf. While called 'Florida' pompano, this silvery beauty actually travels up and down the entire Atlantic coast following warm waters. The city of Pompano Beach, Florida was actually named after this prized fish!
description: The Florida pompano is a sleek, deep-bodied fish with a distinctly compressed, almost disc-like shape and a blunt, rounded snout. Its body shimmers with blue-green tones on top that fade to bright silver or golden-yellow below, with matching yellowish fins. Most pompano you'll encounter are relatively small, weighing less than 3 pounds and measuring under 17 inches, though exceptional individuals can reach up to 26 inches and weigh 8-9 pounds. This is a warm-water fish that occasionally ventures into New England waters during the hottest summer months.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Deeply compressed, almost pancake-flat body that feels firm and muscular when handled, with a distinctly rounded profile that's much taller than it is thick

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Brilliant silver body with blue-green highlights on the back, often showing golden or yellow tints on the sides and belly that seem to glow in sunlight

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small mouth with a very blunt, rounded snout that looks almost stubby compared to the fish's deep body

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Fins have a yellowish tinge and feel relatively soft to the touch, with a deeply forked tail that's proportionally large for the body

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically hand-sized fish, most commonly 12-17 inches long, feeling surprisingly heavy and solid for their length due to the deep body

habitat: In New England waters, Florida pompano are rare summer visitors found in warm coastal areas, particularly around sandy beaches, shallow bays, and near-shore waters. They prefer areas with sandy or muddy bottoms where they can forage for small crustaceans and shellfish. You're most likely to encounter them during unusually warm summers in protected southern New England coastal waters.

seasonality.spring: Absent from New England waters during the cool spring months, as water temperatures are too cold for this warm-water species.
seasonality.summer: Occasionally appears in southern New England waters during the warmest summer months, particularly during heat waves when ocean temperatures peak.
seasonality.fall: May linger into early fall if water temperatures remain warm, but typically begins moving south as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent from New England waters, having migrated south to warmer Atlantic waters off the Carolinas and Florida.

funFact: Florida pompano are so prized as a food fish that they're now being farm-raised in aquaculture operations - but wild pompano can sell for over $20 per pound at high-end restaurants, making them one of the most valuable fish per pound in American waters!
confusionNotes: In New England waters, pompano might be confused with small bluefish or other silvery fish, but the pompano's extremely deep, compressed body and tiny mouth are dead giveaways. Remember: if it looks like someone flattened a dinner plate and gave it fins, it's probably a pompano!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Florida' pompano, this fish is actually found all along the Atlantic coast seasonally. The name simply reflects where they're most abundant and where they spend winter months. In New England, any pompano sighting is noteworthy since they're at the very northern edge of their range.
compareHints: Florida pompano can be distinguished from their close relative, the permit, by their much smaller size and more golden coloration - permits are typically much larger and more silvery. Both have the characteristic deep, compressed body shape, but permits have a more pronounced forehead and can grow much larger, often exceeding 20 pounds compared to the pompano's typical 3-pound size.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Permit are much larger and deeper-bodied than their cousin the Florida pompano, with more dramatically curved fins that sweep back like scythes.
